result:
I want to talk about how absurdly, beautifully weird it is that we’re all just walking around carrying around 86 billion neurons that somehow learned to be self-conscious.

Think about it: a few hundred thousand years ago some nervous ape figured out that if it made a certain sequence of grunts, the other apes would understand that there was a lion nearby. Fast-forward and those same grunts have turned into symphonies, love letters, dad jokes, conspiracy theories, and this very sentence you’re reading right now.

We somehow went from “fire hot, ouch” to debating whether we’re living in a simulation while eating sushi that was flown in from Japan this morning. The sheer ridiculousness of human existence is staggering.

I love that we’re the only species that tells itself stories so convincing we’ll die for them. We fall in love with imaginary people in books. We cry at pixels arranged in a certain way. We spend years of our lives chasing goals that our own future selves might find meaningless. And somehow... that’s the best part.

There’s something sacred about how pointless and magnificent it all is. We’re these tiny, temporary arrangements of stardust that learned how to feel nostalgia for moments that haven’t even ended yet. We build machines that can beat us at chess and then feel proud of the machines. We know we’re going to die and we still plant trees. We write songs about how everything is temporary while knowing the song itself will probably be forgotten in a few generations.

I don’t know. Maybe the meaning of life is just that we keep managing to find it hilarious and heartbreaking at the same time. That we can look at the universe, which clearly doesn’t give a damn about us, and still decide to love it anyway. Still decide to be kind. Still decide to make art and memes and sandwiches and bad decisions and beautiful ones.

We’re all just temporary patterns of consciousness pretending we’re not. And for some reason, that makes me stupidly, irrationally hopeful.

What a time to be a bunch of atoms that learned how to cry at sunsets.
